claims.claim: When cell-cell adhesion is interrupted in the left DM, the cells become more dispersed and extend filopodia over toward the right side, suggesting pathogenic cell migration.
claims.source: In support of this, we have previously shown that when cell-cell adhesion is interrupted in the left DM, the cells become more dispersed (Kurpios et al., 2008; Welsh et al., 2013) and extend filopodia over toward the right side, suggesting pathogenic cell migration (Welsh et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on cell-cell adhesion in the DM.

claims.claim: Lefty1 is expressed at the midline of early embryos (HH9).
claims.source: While Lefty1 was expressed at the midline of early embryos as expected (Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Lefty1 is not expressed at the midline of the DM at HH19.
claims.source: it was not expressed at the midline of the DM at HH19 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) data showed a fibrous matrix between the notochord and endoderm where the DM will later develop.
claims.source: Interestingly, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) data showed a fibrous matrix between the notochord and endoderm where the DM will later develop, suggesting that ECM may separate the two sides before they coalesce into the DM (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SEM data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: Basement membranes are dense ECM requiring laminin, collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan and/or agrin.
claims.source: Basement membranes are dense ECM requiring laminin, collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan and/or agrin (both heparan sulfate proteoglycans) with a large variety of other components that can be integrated to create specific 'flavors' of basement membrane tuned to different barrier contexts (Yurchenco, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on basement membrane composition.

claims.claim: At HH18, laminin IF marked an oval-shaped structure just ventral to the notochord and dorsal to the gut endoderm.
claims.source: At HH18, when cellular DM asymmetries are first being initiated at the level of the midgut (which forms the small intestine), laminin IF marked an oval-shaped structure just ventral to the notochord and dorsal to the gut endoderm (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: No cells were seen within the midline structure at HH18 as shown by a lack of nuclear staining and empty space in SEM.
claims.source: No cells were seen within this structure as shown by a lack of nuclear staining (Figure 3E) and empty space in SEM (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and SEM data shown in Figure 3E, 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: At HH19, the midline structure lengthened, forming two parallel lines connecting the endoderm and notochord.
claims.source: As the DM elongates and asymmetries become more apparent (HH19), this midline structure lengthened, forming two parallel lines connecting the endoderm and notochord (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: At HH20, the midline was still present but began to appear fragmented.
claims.source: One stage later (HH20), the midline was still present but began to appear fragmented (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: By HH21, the midline disappeared while laminin IF underlying the coelomic epithelium and endoderm remained intense.
claims.source: By HH21, the asymmetries of the DM are established—the right DM has expanded, the left DM has condensed, the gut has tilted to the left, and vascular precursor cells have been driven out of the right side (Figure 1B; Mahadevan et al., 2014; Sanketi et al., 2022). Surprisingly, the midline disappeared by this stage, while laminin IF underlying the coelomic epithelium and endoderm remained intense (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3H and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The lengthening of the midline and its subsequent loss occurred in an anterior-to-posterior wave down the embryonic gut tube.
claims.source: The lengthening of the midline and its subsequent loss occurred in an anterior-to-posterior wave down the embryonic gut tube (Figure 3J and K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claims.claim: Nidogen co-localizes with laminin at the midline.
claims.source: To further characterize the nature of the ECM at the DM midline, we did IF staining for nidogen and perlecan, confirming co-localization with laminin at the midline barrier (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Perlecan co-localizes with laminin at the midline.
claims.source: To further characterize the nature of the ECM at the DM midline, we did IF staining for nidogen and perlecan, confirming co-localization with laminin at the midline barrier (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The DM midline consists of basement membrane.
claims.source: This further illustrates that the DM midline consists of basement membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization of laminin, nidogen, and perlecan at the midline, which are foundational basement membrane components.

claims.claim: This basement membrane structure is conserved in the squamate veiled chameleon, C. calyptratus, which exhibits a similarly transient double basement membrane at the midline of the DM from approximately the 7-somite stage to the 29-somite stage.
claims.source: This basement membrane structure is conserved in the squamate veiled chameleon, C. calyptratus, which exhibits a similarly transient double basement membrane at the midline of the DM from approximately the 7-somite stage to the 29-somite stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 4; Diaz et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and a citation to prior work on chameleon development.

claims.claim: Fibronectin localized to the dorsal aorta which often coincides with the most ventral part of the midline.
claims.source: A common basement membrane constituent is fibronectin, which is best known for its role in the provisional matrix during wound healing (Clark et al., 1982). At our developmental stages of interest, fibronectin localized to the dorsal aorta which often coincides with the most ventral part of the midline (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and a citation to prior work on fibronectin.

claims.claim: The midline is sandwiched between mesenchymal cells from the left and right DM, unbiased to either the left or the right side.
claims.source: Although we have established the time kinetics of DM midline formation, the origin of this structure remains elusive. The midline is sandwiched between mesenchymal cells from the left and right DM, unbiased to either the left or the right side (Figure 2F and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell labeling data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claims.claim: Mesenchymal cells are not usually competent to construct an organized basement membrane.
claims.source: Intriguingly, mesenchymal cells like these are not usually competent to construct an organized basement membrane (Yurchenco, 2011; Glentis et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on basement membrane formation.

claims.claim: Mesenchymal cells can secrete matrix components, but the organization of these components into a basement membrane is dependent on the presence of cell surface anchors which are characteristic of tissues like polarized epithelium or endothelium, not mesenchymal cells.
claims.source: Mesenchymal cells can secrete matrix components (Simon-Assmann et al., 1998), but the organization of these components into a basement membrane is dependent on the presence of cell surface anchors which are characteristic of tissues like polarized epithelium or endothelium, not mesenchymal cells (Glentis et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on basement membrane organization.

claims.claim: LAMA1 is secreted by the epithelia in the developing intestine, not the mesenchyme.
claims.source: In the case of LAMA1, it is known that this protein is secreted by the epithelia in the developing intestine, not the mesenchyme (Simon-Assmann et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on LAMA1 expression.

claims.claim: RNA in situ hybridization for Lama1 did not show enriched expression in the mesenchyme at the DM midline.
claims.source: Indeed, RNA in situ hybridization for Lama1 did not show enriched expression in the mesenchyme at the DM midline (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claims.claim: The left coelomic epithelium was polarized at HH19 relative to its basement membrane as quantified by Golgi staining with GM130.
claims.source: As expected, the left coelomic epithelium was polarized at HH19 relative to its basement membrane as quantified by Golgi staining with GM130 (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Welsh et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GM130 staining data shown in Figure 4D and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Cells immediately to the left or right of the midline have random orientation.
claims.source: However, GM130 staining and quantification showed that cells immediately to the left or right of the midline have random orientation (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GM130 staining and quantification data shown in Figure 4D and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Embryos isolated at HH19 and HH21 showed that GFP-labeled endodermal cells remain restricted to the endoderm—there were no GFP+ mesenchymal cells present in the DM.
claims.source: Interestingly, embryos isolated at HH19 and HH21 showed that GFP-labeled cells remain restricted to the endoderm—there were no GFP+ mesenchymal cells present in the DM (Figure 4G and H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by endodermal electroporation and lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claims.claim: The DM midline is not formed from EMT of basement membrane-carrying endodermal cells.
claims.source: This indicates that the DM midline is not formed from EMT of basement membrane-carrying endodermal cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that GFP-labeled endodermal cells do not contribute to the DM mesenchyme.

claims.claim: Laminin IF did not reveal a secondary midline-like structure associated with the ectopic notochord in notochord transplant experiments.
claims.source: Laminin IF did not reveal a secondary midline-like structure associated with the ectopic notochord (Figure 4K and M) while the normal midline was unaffected (Figure 4K and M, white arrows).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by notochord transplant and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4K and M.

claims.claim: The notochord is not sufficient for the formation of DM midline.
claims.source: From this, we conclude that the notochord is not sufficient for the formation of DM midline.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the notochord transplant experiments showing no ectopic midline formation.

claims.claim: NTN4 has very high binding affinity for laminin gamma subunits, such that NTN4 can prevent the formation of new laminin networks and can also disrupt existing laminin networks.
claims.source: NTN4 has very high binding affinity for laminin gamma subunits, such that NTN4 can prevent the formation of new laminin networks, which are the foundation upon which other basement membrane components assemble and can also disrupt existing laminin networks (Schneiders et al., 2007; Reuten et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on NTN4 function.

claims.claim: When Ntn4 was overexpressed on either side of the DM by electroporation, the basement membrane underlying the coelomic epithelium was perturbed and the scattered laminin staining in the mesenchyme was depleted.
claims.source: As expected, when we overexpressed Ntn4 on either side of the DM by electroporation, we perturbed the basement membrane underlying the coelomic epithelium and depleted the scattered laminin staining in the mesenchyme that results from EMT creating the DM (Figure 5B, D, and E vs. controls Figure 5A and C; Horejs, 2016; Hu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Ntn4 overexpression and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B, D, and E compared to controls in Figure 5A and C, and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The DM midline basement membrane remained visibly intact in all embryos with lateral and bilateral Ntn4 overexpression in the DM.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the DM midline basement membrane remained visibly intact in all embryos with lateral (Figure 5B and D) and bilateral (Figure 5E) Ntn4 overexpression in the DM.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Ntn4 overexpression and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B, D, and E.

claims.claim: Endodermal Ntn4 overexpression caused much less disruption of the endodermal or midline basement membranes when compared to its effect on coelomic epithelium basement membrane.
claims.source: Similarly, endodermal Ntn4 overexpression caused much less disruption of the endodermal or midline basement membranes (Figure 5G vs. control Figure 5F) when compared to its effect on coelomic epithelium basement membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by endodermal Ntn4 overexpression and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5G compared to control in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The midline and endoderm may have basement membranes of the same 'flavor', possibly pointing to a common origin.
claims.source: This suggests that the midline and endoderm may have basement membranes of the same 'flavor', possibly pointing to a common origin.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the similar resistance of midline and endodermal basement membranes to NTN4 disruption.

claims.claim: Genes including Cxcl12 and Bmp4 which encode diffusible signals are expressed asymmetrically in the DM.
claims.source: Genes including Cxcl12 (Mahadevan et al., 2014; Sivakumar et al., 2018) and Bmp4 (Sanketi et al., 2022) which encode diffusible signals are expressed asymmetrically in the DM (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6A and B and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Genes encoding enzymes that are secreted into the ECM, like the HA-modifying enzyme TSG6, are expressed asymmetrically in the DM.
claims.source: So too are genes encoding enzymes that are secreted into the ECM, like the HA-modifying enzyme TSG6 (Sivakumar et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on TSG6 expression.

claims.claim: The expression domains of asymmetrically expressed genes have a sharp boundary at the midline, since left and right cells do not mix.
claims.source: The expression domains of these genes have a sharp boundary at the midline, since left and right cells do not mix.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that left and right cells do not mix (Figure 2).

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of pro-angiogenic Cxcl12 on the right side results in an aberrant vessel forming on the right.
claims.source: We know that experimentally mixing left and right signals is detrimental to gut tilting and vascular patterning (Mahadevan et al., 2014; Kurpios et al., 2008; Davis et al., 2008; Welsh et al., 2013; Sivakumar et al., 2018; Sanketi et al., 2022)—e.g., ectopic expression of pro-angiogenic Cxcl12 on the right side results in an aberrant vessel forming on the right (Mahadevan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on Cxcl12 ectopic expression.

claims.claim: When the CXCR4 receptor antagonist AMD3100 is introduced to the left DM, it abolishes vascular development on the left.
claims.source: Moreover, when the CXCR4 receptor antagonist AMD3100 (MW = 502.78) is introduced to the left DM, it abolishes vascular development on the left.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on AMD3100 effects.

claims.claim: When AMD3100 is introduced to the right DM, the left-sided vascular development remains intact.
claims.source: However, when the same drug is introduced to the right DM, the left-sided vascular development remains intact (Mahadevan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on AMD3100 effects.

claims.claim: When 3 kDa fluorescent dextran was injected into the right side of the DM at HH19 when the midline is intact, movement of dextran through the tissue was limited to the right side.
claims.source: When these injections are performed at stages where the midline is intact (HH19), movement of dextran through the tissue was limited to the right side (n=4/4 embryos) (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dextran injection and imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: When the basement membrane midline appears fragmented (HH20), dextran injections produced mixed results—in some embryos, diffusion across the midline was prevented and in others the dextran was able to move into the left mesenchyme of the DM.
claims.source: When the basement membrane midline appears fragmented (HH20), these injections produced mixed results—in some embryos (n=2/9), diffusion across the midline was prevented and in others (n=7/9) the dextran was able to move into the left mesenchyme of the DM (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dextran injection and imaging data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: At stages where no organized basement membrane structure remains at the midline (HH23), diffusion of dextran was always permitted across the entire width of the DM.
claims.source: Finally, at stages where no organized basement membrane structure remains at the midline (HH23), diffusion of dextran was always permitted across the entire width of the DM (n=7/7) (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dextran injection and imaging data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The ratio of average AMD3100-BODIPY intensity in the right DM vs. the left DM was below 0.5 when the midline is intact (HH19), indicating little diffusion across the DM.
claims.source: The ratio of average AMD3100-BODIPY intensity in the right DM vs. the left DM was below 0.5 when the midline is intact (HH19, n=4/4), indicating little diffusion across the DM (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AMD3100-BODIPY beading and imaging data shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: When no midline remains at HH21, the ratio of AMD3100-BODIPY intensity in right vs. left DM significantly rises to near one, indicating diffusion of the drug is not impeded when the midline basement membrane structure is absent.
claims.source: When no midline remains at a later stage (HH21, n=4/4), this ratio significantly rises to near one, indicating diffusion of the drug is not impeded when the midline basement membrane structure is absent (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AMD3100-BODIPY beading and imaging data shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: The basement membrane structure at the midline forms a transient functional barrier against diffusion.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that the basement membrane structure at the midline forms a transient functional barrier against diffusion (Figure 6M).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dextran and AMD3100-BODIPY diffusion experiments.

claims.claim: The brain has the only known organ-specific midline barrier, where commissural axons of the brain and spinal cord are tightly controlled by midline-localized guidance and repulsion cues including FGFs, SLIT/ROBO signaling, EFNB3, heparan sulfate proteoglycans, and the Rac-specific GTPase-activating protein α-chimaerin.
claims.source: Individual organs, too, have LR asymmetries, but the brain has the only known organ-specific midline barrier, where commissural axons of the brain and spinal cord are tightly controlled by midline-localized guidance and repulsion cues including FGFs, SLIT/ROBO signaling, EFNB3, heparan sulfate proteoglycans, and the Rac-specific GTPase-activating protein α-chimaerin (Cavalcante et al., 2002; Kullander et al., 2001; Brose et al., 1999; Kidd et al., 1998; Erskine et al., 2000; Neugebauer and Yost, 2014; Katori et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on brain midline barriers.

claims.claim: Some morphogens (like Nodal) can induce effects at distances of 200 μm or greater.
claims.source: While the diffusion of a given signal depends on the tissue context (Müller et al., 2013). some morphogens (like Nodal) can induce effects at distances of 200 μm or greater (Müller and Schier, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on morphogen diffusion.

claims.claim: The HH19 DM is only about 150 μm across.
claims.source: The HH19 DM is only about 150 μm across, not a prohibitive distance for diffusible signals like BMPs, TGFβ (Sanketi et al., 2022), and CXCL12 (Mahadevan et al., 2014) to cross between the left and right DM.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on measurements of the DM and is used to support the hypothesis that a barrier is needed.

claims.claim: The midline limits diffusion of dextran from right to left, which suggests that it also blocks the movement of endogenous diffusible signals.
claims.source: In support of this, we showed that the midline limits diffusion of dextran from right to left, which suggests that it also blocks the movement of endogenous diffusible signals.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the dextran diffusion experiments.

claims.claim: Dextran's inability to cross the midline indicates that diffusible proteins of typical weight (such as CXCL12 at 10 kDa and BMP4 at 34 kDa) are also unable to cross.
claims.source: Moreover, with a molecular weight of just 3 kDa, dextran's inability to cross the midline indicates that diffusible proteins of typical weight (such as CXCL12 at 10 kDa and BMP4 at 34 kDa) are also unable to cross.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular weight of dextran and the diffusion experiments.

claims.claim: Basement membranes play many critical barrier functions in the embryo and adult, usually found as a single layer that underlies polarized epithelial or endothelial cell layers.
claims.source: Basement membranes play many critical barrier functions in the embryo and adult, usually found as a single layer that underlies polarized epithelial or endothelial cell layers such as those lining the intestines, encircling blood vessels, or enveloping muscle cells, adipocytes, or Schwann cells (Yurchenco, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on basement membrane function and is established knowledge.

claims.claim: Null mutations in genes encoding basement membrane components often result in embryonic lethality and postnatal pathologies.
claims.source: As such, null mutations in genes encoding basement membrane components often result in embryonic lethality and postnatal pathologies (Bader et al., 2005; Miner et al., 2004; Smyth et al., 1999; Gatseva et al., 2019; Pozzi et al., 2017; Yao, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work on basement membrane mutations.

claims.claim: A role for basement membrane in establishing LR asymmetry has not been described previously.
claims.source: However, a role for basement membrane in establishing LR asymmetry has not been described previously.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The basement membrane we describe here is atypical in its double membrane structure.
claims.source: The basement membrane we describe here is atypical in its double membrane structure, which raises interesting questions about its formation.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of the midline basement membrane based on the data presented.

claims.claim: Upon electroporation of the endoderm with GFP, GFP-positive cells were not detected in the DM later in development but remained restricted to the endoderm, indicating that the midline does not form from EMT of basement membrane-carrying endodermal cells.
claims.source: Upon electroporation of the endoderm with GFP, GFP-positive cells were not detected in the DM later in development but remained restricted to the endoderm (Figure 4F–H), indicating that the midline does not form from EMT of basement membrane-carrying endodermal cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by endodermal electroporation and lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claims.claim: There was no appreciable cell death observed by TUNEL staining at the midline during the stages of interest.
claims.source: We can also eliminate endodermal death as a possible mechanism, because there was no appreciable cell death observed by TUNEL staining at the midline during the stages of interest (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on TUNEL staining data that is mentioned but not shown.

claims.claim: The midline does not form in the same way as other double basement membranes, which arise from the meeting of the basal sides of two tissues.
claims.source: Nor does the midline form in the same way as other double basement membranes, which arise from the meeting of the basal sides of two tissues (Keeley and Sherwood, 2019; Pastor-Pareja, 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on double basement membrane formation.

claims.claim: In the case of the DM midline barrier, the apical sides of the endodermal cells are facing each other.
claims.source: Instead in the case of the DM midline barrier, the apical sides of the endodermal cells are facing each other.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on the structure of the DM and endoderm.

claims.claim: The midline forms when basement membrane is left behind as the endoderm descends ventrally during normal development, as if it were a 'scar' of where the endoderm was previously.
claims.source: We hypothesize that the midline forms when basement membrane is left behind as the endoderm descends ventrally during normal development, as if it were a 'scar' of where the endoderm was previously (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and is illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: During early development the notochord is embedded within the endoderm and a basement membrane covers the two structures.
claims.source: During early development the notochord is embedded within the endoderm and a basement membrane covers the two structures. Only later are the two structures separated by a full basement membrane, pointing to a strong connection between the two (Fausett et al., 2014; Jurand, 1974).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on notochord and endoderm development.

claims.claim: The medial migration of the aortae and coelomic epithelia could provide tissue forces that push the notochord and endoderm apart, leaving behind basement membrane at the DM midline.
claims.source: The medial migration of the aortae and coelomic epithelia could provide tissue forces that push the notochord and endoderm apart, leaving behind basement membrane at the DM midline.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claims.claim: The observation that the basement membranes of both the endoderm and midline were resistant to disruption by NTN4 could support the idea that the endoderm is responsible for making both basement membranes.
claims.source: The observation that the basement membranes of both the endoderm and midline were resistant to disruption by NTN4 could also support the idea that the endoderm is responsible for making both basement membranes (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the NTN4 overexpression experiments and is illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The basement membrane underlying the gut endoderm does not co-migrate with the intestinal epithelial cells as they move from the proliferative intestinal crypts to the tip of the villus over the course of 3–6 days in the adult; the basement membrane is instead left in place.
claims.source: In support of this, we know that the basement membrane underlying the gut endoderm does not co-migrate with the intestinal epithelial cells as they move from the proliferative intestinal crypts to the tip of the villus over the course of 3–6 days in the adult; the basement membrane is instead left in place. (Trier et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on intestinal epithelial cell migration.

claims.claim: The endodermal basement membrane and midline's resistance to NTN4 disruption is particularly notable, as similar resistance has not been reported before.
claims.source: The endodermal basement membrane and midline's resistance to NTN4 disruption is particularly notable, as similar resistance has not been reported before.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The resistance of endodermal and midline basement membranes to NTN4 suggests the presence of an unknown factor or modification that shields or stabilizes the laminin network from NTN4 binding.
claims.source: This suggests the presence of an unknown factor or modification that shields or stabilizes the laminin network from NTN4 binding.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the NTN4 overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: The loss of the DM midline barrier may be caused in part by 'stretching' of the basement membrane as the notochord and endoderm become increasingly separated due to the elongation of the DM.
claims.source: We consider that the loss of the DM midline barrier may be caused in part by 'stretching' of the basement membrane as the notochord and endoderm become increasingly separated due to the elongation of the DM (Figure 3J).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and is illustrated in Figure 3J.

claims.claim: The turnover of stable basement membranes occurs on the scale of weeks, but the midline barrier appears to degrade over just 12–24 hr.
claims.source: The turnover of stable basement membranes occurs on the scale of weeks (Trier et al., 1990; Decaris et al., 2014), but the midline barrier appears to degrade over just 12–24 hr.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on basement membrane turnover and observations of midline degradation kinetics.

claims.claim: Basement membrane destruction can occur over a large area, such as by secretion of matrix metalloproteinases in metastasizing cancer.
claims.source: In other contexts, basement membrane destruction can occur over a large area, such as by secretion of matrix metalloproteinases in metastasizing cancer (Miyoshi et al., 2004; Miyoshi et al., 2005)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on basement membrane destruction in cancer.

claims.claim: Basement membrane destruction can be more localized, as exhibited by invadopodia on immune or cancer cells before metastasis.
claims.source: or more localized, as exhibited by invadopodia on immune or cancer cells before metastasis (Sekiguchi and Yamada, 2018; Santiago-Medina et al., 2015).

claims.source: In mammals, prior studies have observed midline laminin deposition in the mouse gut located between the separating notochord and endoderm, further suggesting conservation of a midline basement membrane in amniotes (Li et al., 2007; Hajduk et al., 2012).

results.result: A transient double basement membrane structure forms at the midline of the dorsal mesentery (DM) during embryonic development. This structure is marked by laminin, nidogen, and perlecan, appears at HH18 as an oval structure, lengthens into two parallel lines at HH19, fragments at HH20, and disappears by HH21 in an anterior-to-posterior wave.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C32, C42-C50, and C89 collectively demonstrate the existence and temporal dynamics of the midline basement membrane through immunofluorescence data (Figures 3E-H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), SEM imaging (Figure 3C-D), and quantification (Figure 3I-K). The co-localization of foundational basement membrane components (laminin, nidogen, perlecan) provides strong evidence for the structure's identity as basement membrane.

results.result: Left and right cells of the DM originate from bilateral EMT of the coelomic epithelium and meet at the midline but do not mix, despite the absence of a visible histological boundary at HH20-21.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 and C53 are supported by dye injection experiments (Figure 2C-F), electroporation-based lineage tracing (Figure 2G-H), and H&E staining (Figure 2K-L). The data consistently show segregation of left and right cell populations, which is well-documented in prior work and confirmed by the current experiments.

results.result: The midline basement membrane functions as a transient barrier against diffusion. When intact at HH19, it prevents diffusion of 3 kDa dextran and AMD3100-BODIPY across the DM. When fragmented (HH20) or absent (HH21-23), diffusion is permitted.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 are supported by dextran injection experiments (Figure 6D-G) and AMD3100-BODIPY beading assays (Figure 6H-L) with appropriate sample sizes (n=4-9 per condition). The temporal correlation between midline integrity and diffusion restriction is statistically significant (p<0.0001 for AMD3100-BODIPY at HH19 vs HH21). The experiments provide direct functional evidence for barrier activity.

results.result: The midline basement membrane is resistant to disruption by Netrin4 (Ntn4) overexpression, unlike the coelomic epithelium basement membrane. The endodermal basement membrane shows similar resistance, suggesting a common 'flavor' or origin.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C64-C68 are supported by Ntn4 overexpression experiments (Figure 5) showing selective disruption of coelomic epithelium basement membrane while midline and endodermal basement membranes remain intact. The resistance is observed in lateral (n=5), bilateral (n=3), and endodermal (n=8) electroporations. This differential susceptibility provides evidence for distinct basement membrane compositions.

results.result: Lefty1 is expressed at the midline of early embryos (HH9) but not at the DM midline at HH19, indicating a different mechanism operates during gut asymmetry establishment.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by RNA in situ hybridization data (Figure 3A-B) showing Lefty1 expression at the early embryonic midline but absence at the DM midline during the critical stages of asymmetry establishment. This finding is important for distinguishing the DM midline mechanism from the early embryonic Lefty1-based barrier.

results.result: The midline is not produced by mesenchymal cells adjacent to it. Mesenchymal cells lack the polarization and expression patterns needed for basement membrane organization, and Lama1 is not enriched at the midline mesenchyme.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 and C61 are supported by RNA in situ hybridization for Lama1 (Figure 4A-C), GM130 polarity analysis (Figure 4D-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and citations to prior work on basement membrane formation. The quantitative polarity analysis (n=5 embryos, 346 left margin cells, 413 right margin cells) shows random orientation (p=0.40 and p=0.98 respectively), contrasting with polarized coelomic epithelium (p<0.0001).

results.result: The midline does not form from EMT of endodermal cells. Endodermal electroporation with GFP shows labeled cells remain restricted to the endoderm at HH19 and HH21 with no GFP+ mesenchymal cells in the DM.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 and C90 are supported by endodermal electroporation and lineage tracing experiments (Figure 4F-H) showing GFP-labeled endodermal cells do not contribute to the DM mesenchyme (n=8 at HH19, n=2 at HH21). This rules out one potential mechanism for midline formation.

results.result: The notochord is not sufficient for DM midline formation. Ectopic notochord transplants do not induce secondary midline-like structures, while the normal midline remains unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by notochord transplant experiments (Figure 4I-M) with appropriate controls (chordin RNA in situ to confirm transplant viability) and laminin immunofluorescence showing no ectopic midline formation (n=8). This rules out notochord sufficiency for midline induction.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that the midline forms when basement membrane is left behind as the endoderm descends ventrally, like a 'scar' of where the endoderm was previously. This is supported by the early association of notochord and endoderm, tissue forces from aortic and coelomic epithelial migration, and similar NTN4 resistance of endodermal and midline basement membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 represent a hypothesis based on indirect evidence including the NTN4 resistance similarity (Figure 5), early notochord-endoderm association (citations), and anatomical observations. While the hypothesis is plausible and supported by circumstantial evidence, direct demonstration of basement membrane 'left behind' by descending endoderm is lacking. The proposed mechanism requires additional experimental validation such as basement membrane component tracing.

results.result: The midline basement membrane structure is conserved in the veiled chameleon (C. calyptratus), exhibiting a similarly transient double basement membrane from approximately the 7-somite to 29-somite stage.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by immunofluorescence data from chameleon embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) at multiple developmental stages (St. 24-25 n=10, St. 26-28 n=9). This demonstrates evolutionary conservation of the structure in amniotes and suggests functional importance.

results.result: Genes encoding diffusible signals (Cxcl12, Bmp4) and secreted enzymes (TSG6) are expressed asymmetrically in the DM with sharp boundaries at the midline. Experimental mixing of left and right signals is detrimental to gut tilting and vascular patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are supported by RNA in situ hybridization data (Figure 6A-B) and citations to prior work demonstrating consequences of signal mixing. The sharp expression boundaries are consistent with the cell segregation data (Figure 2) and provide functional context for why a diffusion barrier would be necessary.

results.result: SEM data shows a fibrous matrix between the notochord and endoderm where the DM will later develop, suggesting ECM may separate the two sides before they coalesce into the DM.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 is supported by SEM imaging (Figure 3C-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing fibrous ECM in the space between notochord and endoderm at early stages (HH15-16). This provides structural evidence for early ECM presence that may contribute to midline formation.

results.result: The loss of the DM midline barrier may be caused by 'stretching' of the basement membrane as the notochord and endoderm become increasingly separated. The midline degrades over 12-24 hours, much faster than typical basement membrane turnover (weeks).
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 present a hypothesis for midline degradation based on the rapid timescale (12-24 hr vs weeks for stable basement membranes) and increasing notochord-endoderm distance. While the temporal observations are supported by the data (Figure 3I), the mechanical stretching mechanism is speculative. Alternative active degradation mechanisms are also discussed but not tested.

results.result: There was no appreciable cell death observed by TUNEL staining at the midline during the stages of interest.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is mentioned but the TUNEL staining data is not shown ('data not shown'). Without access to the actual data, sample sizes, or quantification methods, this claim cannot be properly evaluated. This is a methodological weakness that should be addressed by including the data in supplementary materials.

results.result: Fusion of the aortae coincides with midline fragmentation and disappearance, suggesting these processes may be linked. Aortic fusion timing depends on VEGF, SHH, and BMP-inhibitory gene regulation, and VEGF signaling may affect VE-cadherin localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 note temporal correlation between aortic fusion and midline disappearance (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and cite prior work on aortic fusion mechanisms. However, the causal relationship between these processes is speculative. The correlation is interesting but requires experimental manipulation to establish causality.

results.result: Background on left-right asymmetry establishment in vertebrate development, including the role of the DM in gut looping and vascular patterning, the requirement for a Lefty1+ midline barrier in early embryos, and the brain as the only known organ with an organ-specific midline barrier.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C8-C18 provide established background knowledge supported by extensive citations to prior work. These claims set the context for the current study and are well-supported by the literature. They are not novel findings of this manuscript but are accurately represented.

results.result: Background on gut development and the role of the DM in directing gut looping through left-right asymmetric properties at molecular, cellular, and extracellular levels. The DM also directs asymmetric vascular development.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C31 provide established background on gut development and DM function, supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of DM asymmetries and their functional consequences, setting up the rationale for investigating a midline barrier.

results.result: When cell-cell adhesion is interrupted in the left DM, cells become more dispersed and extend filopodia toward the right side, suggesting pathogenic cell migration.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by citations to prior work from the same laboratory. This provides additional context for why a midline barrier would be functionally important to prevent inappropriate cell mixing.

results.result: Background on basement membrane composition, function, and importance. Basement membranes require laminin, collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan/agrin, and play critical barrier functions. Mutations in basement membrane components often cause embryonic lethality or postnatal pathologies.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C52, C86-C87 provide established knowledge about basement membranes supported by citations to prior work. Claim C52 adds specific data on fibronectin localization to the dorsal aorta (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). These claims provide necessary background for interpreting the midline basement membrane findings.

results.result: A role for basement membrane in establishing LR asymmetry has not been described previously, and the resistance of the midline and endodermal basement membranes to NTN4 disruption has not been reported before.
results.evaluation: Claims C88 and C99 are statements about the novelty of the findings. These are supported by the absence of prior reports in the literature and represent genuine novel contributions of the manuscript.

results.result: The DM midline does not form like other double basement membranes (which arise from meeting of basal sides of two tissues). Instead, the apical sides of endodermal cells face each other.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by citations to prior work on double basement membrane formation and anatomical observations of the DM structure. This distinction is important for understanding the unique nature of the midline basement membrane.

results.result: In the adult intestine, basement membrane underlying the gut endoderm does not co-migrate with epithelial cells as they move from crypts to villus tips over 3-6 days; the basement membrane is left in place.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is supported by a citation to prior work and provides an analogy for how basement membrane might be 'left behind' during endodermal descent in the embryo. This supports the plausibility of the proposed mechanism for midline formation.

results.result: The resistance of endodermal and midline basement membranes to NTN4 suggests the presence of an unknown factor or modification that shields or stabilizes the laminin network from NTN4 binding.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is a speculation based on the NTN4 resistance observations. While the speculation is reasonable, no experimental evidence is provided to identify or characterize such a factor. This represents an interesting direction for future research but remains unsubstantiated.

results.result: Background on basement membrane breakdown in various contexts (cancer metastasis, developmental processes like mouth opening, corpus callosum formation, optic cup fusion). In all cases, breakdown is spatially specific with neighboring basement membranes unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C111 provide background on basement membrane breakdown mechanisms supported by citations to prior work. Claim C110 adds the observation that the DM midline shows similar spatial specificity (Figure 3H). These comparisons provide context for interpreting midline degradation.

results.result: Background on the role of axial structures in organ development. The heart, lungs, and kidneys rely on dorsal midline structures. Loss of midline structures like the notochord causes defects such as horseshoe kidney due to lack of Shh signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C115 provide background on midline structure importance in organ development, supported by citations to prior work. This contextualizes the potential broader significance of the DM midline barrier beyond gut development.

results.result: The aorta begins as two parallel tubes with an avascular zone between them (where the midline is), then progressively fuses into one with an anterior-to-posterior wave until the level of the vitelline arteries.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is supported by citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 3. This provides important anatomical context for understanding the relationship between the midline and aortic development.

results.result: The condensed left DM is significantly stiffer than the expanded right DM at HH21, and proper gut tilting depends on this difference. The midline barrier may help segregate stiffness-influencing components and provide a 'wall' for the right side to push against.
results.evaluation: Claim C120 is supported by citation to prior work on DM stiffness. Claim C121 is speculation about the midline's mechanical role based on this prior work and the current findings. While plausible, no direct mechanical measurements or manipulations of the midline are performed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: Vascular endothelial cells migrate from right to left adjacent to the endoderm but do not traverse the midline. N-cadherin expression is symmetric when the midline is intact but becomes left-specific upon midline disintegration, suggesting a shift in cell segregation mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124 are supported by citations to prior work from the same laboratory. These observations provide additional functional context for the midline barrier's role in maintaining left-right compartmentalization and suggest temporal coordination between different segregation mechanisms.

results.result: Gut looping patterns are stereotypical within species but vary between species. While differential growth rates are the primary mechanism, modifications to DM asymmetry kinetics and midline barrier properties may provide additional evolutionary tuning of looping patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 are supported by citations to prior work. Claims C127-C128 are speculations about evolutionary implications of the midline barrier. While interesting, these evolutionary hypotheses are not tested and would require comparative studies across species with different gut looping patterns.

results.result: Prior studies have observed midline laminin deposition in the mouse gut between the separating notochord and endoderm, suggesting conservation of a midline basement membrane in amniotes.
results.evaluation: Claim C129 is supported by citations to prior work on mouse gut development. This provides additional evidence for evolutionary conservation of the midline structure beyond the chicken and chameleon data presented in the manuscript.

results.result: Some morphogens like Nodal can induce effects at distances of 200 μm or greater. The HH19 DM is only about 150 μm across, not prohibitive for diffusible signals to cross. The midline's ability to block 3 kDa dextran suggests larger proteins like CXCL12 (10 kDa) and BMP4 (34 kDa) also cannot cross.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 combine citations to prior work on morphogen diffusion with measurements of DM width and inferences from the dextran diffusion experiments. The logic is sound: if 3 kDa dextran cannot cross, larger proteins are also likely blocked. However, direct testing with the endogenous proteins would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: The authors propose that the atypical midline basement membrane forms the boundary between left and right sides and functions as a barrier necessary to establish and protect organ asymmetry.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 represents the main conclusion of the manuscript, integrating the structural characterization (basement membrane composition, temporal dynamics), functional evidence (diffusion barrier), and cellular observations (cell segregation). This conclusion is well-supported by the collective evidence from multiple experimental approaches, though some mechanistic details remain to be elucidated.

results.result: The authors identify a transient double basement membrane structure at the midline of the dorsal mesentery (DM) in chick embryos. This structure is characterized by laminin, nidogen, and perlecan immunofluorescence, appears at HH18 as an oval structure, lengthens into two parallel lines at HH19, fragments at HH20, and disappears by HH21. The structure is acellular and occurs in an anterior-to-posterior wave along the gut tube.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the evidence for the midline structure's dynamics, composition, and transient nature as 'solid' and 'convincing.' They specifically note that immunofluorescence data 'convincingly show the chemical composition of this midline structure as a double basement membrane and its transient existence during the left-right patterning of the dorsal mesentery.' The reviewers affirm this as a 'fundamental discovery' and a 'strong and elegant paper discovering a novel midline structure.'

results.result: The midline basement membrane functions as a physical barrier that prevents cell mixing between left and right DM populations and limits diffusion of molecules across the midline. Dextran and AMD3100-BODIPY diffusion experiments demonstrate that when the midline is intact (HH19), diffusion is blocked, but when it fragments (HH20) or disappears (HH21-23), diffusion is permitted.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state that 'labelling experiments demonstrate a physical and chemical barrier function, to cell mixing and signal diffusion in the dorsal mesentery.' The functional barrier data is described as part of the 'solid' and 'convincing' evidence supporting the midline's role. The reviewers acknowledge this as demonstrating both physical and chemical barrier properties.

results.result: The midline basement membrane is resistant to disruption by Netrin4 (Ntn4) overexpression, unlike the coelomic epithelium basement membrane which is disrupted by Ntn4. The endodermal basement membrane shows similar resistance to Ntn4, suggesting the midline and endoderm may share a common basement membrane 'flavor' or origin.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that the authors use 'well thought tools' to characterize the midline's properties. The Ntn4 resistance data is part of the evidence reviewers cite when stating 'based on laminin expression pattern and Ntn4 resistance, the authors propose a model, whereby the midline basement membrane is progressively deposited by the descending endoderm.' This indicates acceptance of the Ntn4 resistance findings as supporting evidence.

results.result: A similar transient double basement membrane structure at the DM midline is observed in the veiled chameleon (C. calyptratus), suggesting conservation of this mechanism in birds and reptiles.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'observations of a transient midline basement membrane in the veiled chameleon suggest a conserved mechanism in birds and reptiles.' This indicates acceptance of the comparative data as supporting conservation of the structure.

results.result: The origin of the midline basement membrane is investigated through multiple approaches: Lefty1 is not expressed at the DM midline at HH19; Lama1 is not enriched in mesenchyme at the midline; endodermal lineage tracing shows no EMT contribution to the DM; notochord transplants do not induce ectopic midline formation; and TUNEL staining shows no cell death at the midline.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'investigation of its origin and impact on asymmetric organogenesis remains challenging and is not yet conclusive.' They note that 'cell labelling and graft experiments rule out a cellular composition of the midline from dorsal mesenchyme or endoderm origin and rule out an inducing role by the notochord,' but emphasize that 'further work will be necessary to conclude on the origin.' The reviewers acknowledge the authors 'have made several attempts to answer these questions by different means' but the origin remains unresolved.

results.result: The authors propose a model for midline formation in which basement membrane is left behind as a 'scar' when the endoderm descends ventrally during development, potentially driven by medial migration of aortae and coelomic epithelia. The similar Ntn4 resistance of endodermal and midline basement membranes supports a common endodermal origin. The mechanism of midline breakdown may involve stretching as the notochord and endoderm separate, though the rapid degradation (12-24 hr) suggests active processes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'based on laminin expression pattern and Ntn4 resistance, the authors propose a model, whereby the midline basement membrane is progressively deposited by the descending endoderm.' However, they emphasize this is a proposed model and that 'further work will be necessary to conclude on the origin.' The reviewers acknowledge 'the article includes an interesting discussion about these points and the mechanism of midline breakdown,' indicating these are hypotheses rather than established conclusions.

results.result: The authors discuss potential functional implications of the midline, including its temporal correlation with aortic fusion, possible role in segregating mechanical properties (stiffness) between left and right DM, prevention of endothelial cell crossing, and a shift from basement membrane-mediated to N-cadherin-mediated cell segregation after midline disappearance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state that 'further work will be necessary to conclude on the origin and impact of the midline for asymmetric organogenesis.' While they acknowledge the work 'significantly advances our understanding of left-right asymmetric organogenesis, by identifying an organ-specific and stage-specific midline barrier,' the specific functional impacts discussed remain speculative. The reviewers note these are part of 'an interesting discussion' but do not affirm these as established findings.
